# Will It Be Harder for Me?

> "...he makes his sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the just and the unjust."
>
> — Matthew 5:45

No two men come to this book from the same place. One is nineteen and one is sixty. One is married, one has never been kissed. Some situations do look harder than others. They needn't be, once the Big Monster is gone. Take a few examples.

## The man at the front of the church {-}

You'd think it would be easiest for the pastor, the elder, the worship leader, the youth worker. Who knows better than he does what Scripture says about lust? Who has stronger reasons?

But reasons were never the problem. Chapter 1 told you that every extra reason to stop makes stopping harder, and the church leader has more reasons than anyone. Here is how it works against him.

1. **He lives with the fear of being found out.** He fears for his ministry, his income and his family's home. Fear sends a man reaching for comfort, and you know which comfort he has trained himself to use.
2. **His work is draining, and he has nowhere to put it down.** He carries other people's griefs all week. Often he has no pastor of his own.
3. **He believes he must set an example.** So on top of the ordinary guilt he carries a second helping: "I, of all people." The pressure makes him feel more deprived on the days he holds out and more worthless on the days he doesn't. In the end he wonders whether grace still applies to him.
4. **Sunday night.** He has given out all day. The house goes quiet, the tension drops, and that is the hour the habit has claimed for years. Because the relief of the day being over and the act arrive together, the act gets the credit for the relief. The same thing happens to any man who has to go long stretches without, such as the soldier or the man who shares a room. The rare occasion starts to look precious.

On the Willpower Method this man sits through Sunday night feeling robbed of his "one release". But what he actually enjoys on a Sunday night is the rest: the work done, the quiet house, the armchair. None of that goes away. Take the lie out and he can enjoy every bit of it, even with the Little Monster still muttering.

One Christian writer who has been through it says, "Having experienced the prison of masturbation myself, I understand the struggle." If you lead in a church, you're in an ordinary trap, and it opens the ordinary way.

## The man who has been at it for decades {-}

He's sure it must be harder for him. Thirty years of rut can't be the same as three.

It is the same. The Little Monster is no bigger at fifty than he was at fifteen, and the lies are the same lies. Under one man's testimony a commenter did the sum on his own life: from thirteen to forty-four, more than thirty years of it. He was writing at forty-eight. Remember the man from the introduction, free in his forty-third year. The length of the sentence has nothing to do with how the door opens. All it changes is the size of the relief.

## The student and the single man {-}

The other hard-looking case is boredom mixed with stress. Think of the student in exam season, whose work is both tedious and frightening, or the single man in a flat by himself. Each has long empty hours and nobody around.

On the Willpower Method those hours are deadly. He's got all evening to sit and brood over what he's "lost", the brooding makes him low, and being low is a cue. A man on a Christian recovery blog was in exactly that place: "i always blame myself but still its hard for me to leave".

With the right frame of mind those same hours are no trouble. Don't worry that being alone keeps reminding you that you've stopped. Let it. Every reminder is a chance to think: *I'm getting rid of it. Isn't that marvellous?* Thought of that way, the urges turn into small moments of pleasure.

So, will it be harder for you? No. Young or old, married or single, pastor or plumber, believer or not: any man can find this easy and even enjoyable. He only has to follow all the instructions.

## The two main reasons men fail {-}

There are only two worth worrying about.

**The first is something outside you.** A scene in a film, an advert, a photo in your feed, a woman at the gym. Or it's a softer thing: you see a couple holding hands and feel a stab of envy. It catches you in a weak moment. We've been over this at length. When it happens, use it. Remind yourself that there's no such thing as one look or one time. Be glad the chain is broken. And remember that the man still in the trap would swap places with you tomorrow. He's the one to feel sorry for, because he still has to.

**The second is a bad day.** Get this clear before you start: you will have good days and bad days whether you go back to it or not. Jesus said the Father "sends rain on the just and the unjust". It rains on the free man and on the man in the trap. You can't have hills without valleys.

The trouble with the Willpower Method is what the man does with his bad day. He starts pining for his comfort, and now he has two problems. The free man has one. He is also better equipped to meet it, with more energy and a clear head, and he isn't dragging a guilty secret through it.

If a bad day lands on you in the first weeks, shrug and take the punch. You had bad days before, plenty of them, or you wouldn't be reading this book. Then say it plainly: "All right, today is rotten. Jerking off won't fix it. Nor will a video, or a message to her. Tomorrow will be better, and in the meantime I've got one enormous thing going for me. I'm free."

While you're in the trap, you have to shut your eyes to what the habit costs you. You're never foggy and flat, you're just "a bit tired this week". Once you stop, the temptation runs the other way, and you blame everything that goes wrong on having stopped.

So the boss tears a strip off you and you think, "On a night like this I'd have had my release." True. But you've forgotten that it never solved a single problem you brought to it. The boss was still there in the morning. All you're doing is punishing yourself by pining for a prop that never held any weight. It puts you in an impossible position: miserable because you can't, and certain to be worse off if you do.

Your decision was right, and you know it. Why torture yourself by doubting it?

Stay glad. It matters on the good days, and it matters most on the bad ones.
